ImageDescription.value: Line patterns caused by tip/hub vortex. Windpark Japons observed from a distance of ~50 kilometers. In the photograph, the vortex of slowed-down, compressed air is visible as a misty haze trailing behind the turbine, bordered by darker and/or lighter lines or patterned artifacts at the edges of the rotor (tip vortex) and behind the nacelle (hub vortex). Under favorable conditions, from June to September, in the case of a wind farm with a capacity of hundreds of MW, these turbulences—composed of tens or hundreds of vortices behind each individual turbine—reach the rising condensation level (1,000 to 3,000 m) at a distance of 20 to 50 kilometers from the wind farm. They then transform into rapidly intensifying cumulonimbus clouds, rising steeply at an angle of 50–60° to an altitude of over 7,000 m, while rotational movements and wind shear continue to act at the center of this cloud. As a result, the clouds below the cumulonimbus in the lower condensation layer also begin to rotate. A tornado forms.
